translation_clauses.raw_clause: §1 When in former times the sages created [astronomical] systems, they watched the turning of the xuan ji, the motions of the Three Luminaries, the expansion and contraction of the Roads, the growing and shrinking of the shadow, the establishment of the Dipper mainstay, and the orbit of the Caerulean Dragon.
The Three [Luminaries] and the Five [Planets] changed [their positions], and they wove together the numbers, so that they were able to make them into methods [for calculation].

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: This introduction underlines a radical difference of approach between its authors and Liu Xin, creator of the Triple Concordance system.
Whereas he claimed to have derived the constants of his system from cosmological con- siderations, this system claims that its basic data are drawn from observation.
This approach, it is claimed, represents a return to the practice of the ancient sages who created human culture in the mythical past.
Some of the terms used here require a little explanation.
‘ Xuan ji’ refers to the pole star of the Han period, β Ursae minoris;
the changing meanings of this term are discussed in (Cullen, Christopher and Farrer, Anne S.
L.
the ‘Three Luminaries’ are the sun, moon and stars;
the ‘Roads’ are the paths of the sun and moon;
the ‘Establishment of the Dipper’ refers to the changing directions indicated by the handle of the Dipper when first seen at dusk in successive months (see section § 3);

the ‘Caerulean Dragon’, which more usually refers to one of the four creatures associated with groups of constellations correlated with the four directions here refers to the sexagenary name of the year (see sections § 5 and § 18).

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §2 In the movement of Heaven, the turning in one day and night is more than a circuit.
The stars follow Heaven in moving westwards, while the sun goes against Heaven in moving eastwards.
The motion of the sun and its turning round its circuit forms the du in Heaven and the days in the system.
It dwells in the ordered lodges, which terminate in four sevens;
it is received in the cyclical signs, which terminate in six decades.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: The expression ‘one day and night’ refers to a complete solar day, in which the sun returns to the same position relative to the observer.
If we count from the moment of noon, this is the interval between two instants when the sun is on the meridian due south of the observer.
If we count from the moment of midnight, the sun is still crossing the meridian line, but below the horizon in the north.

The statement that ‘the turning in one day and night is more than a circuit’ refers to the fact that since the sun is moving from west to east against the background of the celestial sphere with the fixed stars (which turns from east to west), it follows that from one noon to the next (or one midnight to the next), since the sun has returned to the same position relative to the observe, the celestial sphere has turned a full revolution, plus the sun’s daily motion, which is in fact 1 du.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §3 ‘The sun and moon push one another on’.
The sun is slow and the moon is fast.
When they share a position, that is called a conjunction.
The slow [i.e. the sun] is ahead and the fast [i.e. the moon] is behind.
When they are one part near and three parts distant, that is called a crescent.
When they are opposite one another, so that they divide Heaven down the middle, that is called opposition.
When the fast reaches the slow, so that its bril - liance is exhausted and its form is hidden, that is called darkening [as on the last day of a lunar month].
When darkening and conjunction have joined and separated, and the Dipper Establishment shifts by a sign, that is called a month.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §4 Through the motion of the sun and moon, there is winter and there is sum - mer.
Between winter and summer, there is spring and there is autumn.
Thus when the sun moves through the northern regions, that is called winter;
through the western regions it is called spring;
through the southern regions it is called summer, and through the eastern regions it is called autumn.
When the sun’s path extends out southwards, it goes ever further from the pole, and the shadow becomes ever longer, and when distance and length reach their extreme, then winter culminates there.
When the sun’s path draws in towards the north, it goes ever closer to the pole, and the shadow is ever shorter, and when nearness and shortness reach their extreme, then summer culminates there.
Between the two extremes [sc.
‘solstices’], the path is even and the shadow is true, and spring and autumn are divided there.
The ‘regions’ through which the sun moves are the four quarters of the heavenly sphere corresponding to its position during the four seasons.
The labelling as ‘north’ and so forth in the third sentence is conventional rather than directional.
The meaning becomes literal in the rest of the section, where it is stated that when the sun is at its northernmost the season is summer, and when it is at its southernmost the seasons is winter.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §5 The sun circuits round Heaven:

there is one cold and one heat, the four seasons are all complete, the myriad creatures are all changed, the sheti [i.e. the 12 cyclical characters referring to years] shift their station, and the Cae - rulean Dragon [i.e. the sexagenary name of the year] moves its mark-point.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: This is called a sui.
The head of the sui is the [winter] solstice, and the head of the yue is the conjunction.
When the solstice and the conjunction fall on the same day, that is called a Rule [Head].When this takes place at the head of a day [i.e. midnight], this is called an Obscuration [Head].
When an Obscuration has terminated the six decades, that is called an Era [Head].
When the sui and the conjunction both return, that is called an Origin [Head].

So for the day one fills it, for the yue one intercalates it, for the season one divides it, for the sui one circuits it, for the Rule one illuminates it, for the Obscuration one sections it, for the Era one records it, and for the Origin one traces it to the source.

Only when this is done, then even if there are transformations and a myriad variations, and expansions and contraction without limitation, then there is nothing that is not bound up with these and are endowed and rectified by them.

I have deliberately refrained from providing a translation of the term ‘ sui’ 歲 and ‘yue’ 月 in this section, which illustrates rather well the double reference involved in the use of these words, as was discussed in Chapt er 1.
In its first occurrence ‘sui’ evidently refers to the calendrical unit that we may call the civil year, normally consisting of 12 whole months of either 29 or 30 whole days each.

However, we are next told that the ‘sui’ starts at winter solstice – which is by no means always the case for the civil year, so that the reference is clearly to what I have chosen to call the ‘solar cycle’.

As already explained, in the period covered by this book it was assumed that the winter solstice was at a fixed position relative to the stars, so that (in modern terms) the tropical and sidereal years were equal.
Similar considerations apply to the choice between the translations ‘month’ and ‘lunation’ for yue 月.

When the sun is situated there it is the winter solstice:
that is the time when all things begin to be produced.

Thus the head of the pitch-pipes is Yellow Bell, [astronomical] systems begin from winter solstice, the months give precedence to the establishment zi [the 11th month in the ‘Xia’ count used today, the first Celestial month], and time of day is made even with midnight.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §36 In producing the numbers for lunar eclipses, one records instances where the lunar eclipse is total.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: This is how the figures work out:
The notion of a cycle of 23 lunar eclipses in 135 months predates the Eastern Han.
The cycle begins with a lunar eclipse at the full moon of the first month of the cycle, and the last eclipse falls at the full moon of the 131st month.
The next lunar eclipse is at full moon of the first month of the next 135- month cycle.
135/23 = 5 + 20/23, so this is the mean number of months between eclipses – although actual eclipses must of course be separated by whole numbers of months, since they must fall at full moon.
The mean number of months in a civil year taken over a complete Rule of 19 years is 235/19.
So the mean number of eclipses per year is given by:
(235/19) / (135/23) = (235 × 23) / (19 × 135) Dividing top and bottom by 5, we obtain:
(47 × 23) / (19 × 27) = 1081/513 = 2 + 55/513 which is the mean number of eclipses in one year.
Now an Obscuration is 4 × 19 = 76 years So in an Obscuration, the number of eclipses is:
Note that since there are 940 months in an Obscuration, 27 Obscurations contains:
27 × 940/135 = 188 cycles of 135 months, each with 23 eclipses in the same pattern.
27 Obscurations is 27 × 76 = 27 × 4 × 19 = 2052 years.
This is an Obscura - tion Coincidence.
However 2052 mod 60 = 12, so the sexagenary year number of successive Obscuration Coincidences will shift by this amount.
Taking 5 Obscuration Coincidences would bring return of the sexagenary year number, but the result would not yet be a multiple of the Origin Factor (4560).
This results when we take 4 × 5 = 20 Obscuration Coincidences since:

20 × 2052 = 41,040 = 9 × 4560 At the interval of 41,040 years we therefore have a repetition of lunar eclipse at full moon of the first Celestial month, commencing with coincidence of conjunction, midnight and winter solstice with repetition of sexagenary day name and sexagenary year-name.
This interval is Origin Coincidence.

The aim of this section is to find the sexagenary number (year-name) of the year now beginning.
We do this by finding the sexagenary number of the first year of the current Obscuration, and then counting forward.
The requisite data are provided in Table 3.1.
First we cast out whole Origins, since all relevant conditions repeat in an Origin.
Since an Origin is three Eras, we then establish which of the three Eras of the current Origin we are in.
That tells us which of the three main columns (in the modern format – rows in the original) we should be using.
The columns are named after Heaven, Earth and Man – Celestial, Terrestrial and Anthropic.
Each column has in its first row the sexagenary number of its first year.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §46 Set out the years into the Obscuration and subtract one.
Multiply by Rule Months [235].
Count one for each Rule Factor [19] filled.
Call this Accu- mulated Months.
The remainder is the Intercalation Remainder.
If it is 12 or more, this year has an intercalation.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: This section and the next aim to predict the sexagenary day name of the first day of the first month of the current year according to the Celestial count.
We start from the beginning of the current Obscuration, at which we are guaranteed that midnight, conjunction beginning the first Celestial month and winter solstice coin- cide.
We already know (from Proc. 3.3) the sexagenary day name with which the Obscuration begins.
Here we aim to find how many whole months have elapsed since the start of the Obscuration, and to predict whether the current civil year has an intercalary month or not.
The first procedure deals with the fact that ‘years into the obscuration’ 入 蔀 年 means the ordinal number of year in the Obscuration.
Since we want the number of years from the start of the Obscuration to the start of the current year, we have to subtract one from this number.
Then we use the fact that 235 months are exactly equivalent to 19 years to find how many whole months have elapsed since the start of the Obscuration.
The remainder will be a fraction of a month at a scale of Rule Factor [19].

This is the Intercalation Remainder, and may be taken as the pending fraction of a new intercalary month representing the amount by which the start of the new year is in advance of its ideal date, which should coincide with winter solstice.
Now since 235/19 is 12 + 7/19, it is clear that by the end of the year we are now starting the Intercalation Remainder will have increased by 7.

So if at the start of the current year this Remainder is 12 or more, the Remainder will at least have reached 19 by the end of the year, calling for a delay of a whole month before the next year starts – which requires an intercalary month to be inserted in the current year, as stated.
The Intercalation Remainder will also be useful in later calculations.
In that con - nection, it should be noted that it can also be explained in connection with the sequence of Medial Qi, which begins each year with the Winter Solstice.
At the start of a Rule, winter solstice coincides with the conjunction beginning the Celestial First Month.

This condition recurs at the beginning of the next Rule 19 years later, but the conjunction with which the first winter solstice of that Rule coincides is seven later than the one that would have been indicated if winter solstices were separated by exactly 12 lunations each.

So each successive winter solstice is 7/19 of a lunation later than its predecessor with respect to its Celestial First Month conjunction, and it is the total of this lag that is represented by Intercalation Remainder.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §47 Set out the Accumulated Months into the Obscuration.
Multiply by Obscura - tion Days [27,759].
Count one for each Obscuration Months [940] filled.
Call that Accumulated Days.
The remainder is the Lesser Remainder.
Cast out 60 from the Accumulated Days.
The remainder is the Greater Remainder.
Count off from the [sexagenary] name of the Obscuration, and outside the exhausted count will be the day of Celestial Standard Conjunction in the eleventh [civil] month preceding the [civil] year.
If the Lesser Remainder is 441 or greater, the month is long.
To find the conjunction day of the next month, add 29 to the Greater Remainder, and 499 to the Lesser Remainder.
Count one each time the Lesser Remainder fills Obscuration Months [940].
Take that unit up to the Greater Remainder.
Count off as before.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: We now use the previous result to find the actual day of the Celestial Standard Conjunction, which begins the first Celestial month.
First we convert the Accu- mulated Months into days by using the fact that 27,759 days are precisely equal to 940 months.
The whole days resulting from this procedure tell us how many whole days have elapsed from the midnight commencing the current Obscuration up to midnight beginning the current year.

Since we are interested in sexagenary day names, we can usefully cast out 60 from this amount to form the Greater Remainder as specified in order to find the sexagenary day name of the first day of the current year.
To take an example:
if we are in the second year of the Obscuration, Accumulated Months will be 12.
Since:

12 × 27,759/940 = 354 remainder 348 and 354 mod 60 = 54 the Greater Remainder is 54, so the sexagenary day name of the first day of this year will be 54 further on than the sexagenary day name of the first day of the Obscura- tion.

Note that the text does not treat this as a simple addition – we are to start counting from 1 to 54, starting at the sexagenary day name of the first day of the Obscuration, and then the day name after we finish (‘exhaust’) the count will be the one required.
It is assumed but not stated that if the sexagenary day name passes 60 we shall start again at 1.
In our example, the Lesser Remainder 348 is the fraction of a day at a scale of Obscuration Months [940] left when months are converted to days.
It rep - resents the fraction of a day after midnight when the mean conjunction falls.
Now, since 27,759/940 = 29 + 499/940, the Greater Remainder will increase by 29 each month, and the Lesser Remainder by 499, as stated.

If the Lesser Remainder at the start of the month is already at least 940 − 499 = 441, then clearly the mean conjunction will fall at least a whole day after midnight at the start of the next month, and we shall have to wait 30 rather than 29 days for that month to begin, so that the current month is long, rather than a short 29 days.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §50 Subtract the Intercalation Remainder from Rule Factor [19].
Multiply the remainder by 12.
Count one for each completed Rule Intercalation Number [7];
for a completed four also get one count.
Start from the eleventh month preceding this year;
the month outside the exhausted count is the intercalary month.
[Thus] there may be adjustments back and forth, and these are determined by [the position of] the Medial qi.
In Proc. 3.5, it was determined whether the current year contains an intercalary month.
If there is an intercalary month, this procedure finds where it will come in the sequence of months.
The key to making this decision is to look for a luna - tion within which no medial qi is located.
That lunation normally corresponds to an intercalary month – with, as we shall see, a slight adjustment to allow for certain borderline conditions.
We begin by finding Intercalation Remainder, the remainder from:
(Years into Obscuration) × 235/19.

The whole number result of this division is the total number of whole mean lunations elapsed from the start of the current Obscuration up to the conjunc - tion which began the current (Celestial) year, which will include some lunations corresponding to intercalations in previous years.

The remainder represents the amount in (1/19) of a mean lunation by which the winter solstice near the beginning of this year lags behind the conjunction of the first Celestial month, and this increases by (7/19) of a lunation from one winter solstice to the next.
Now there are 12 medial qi in a year.
So the lag between a medial qi and its preceding conjunction must increase steadily from medial qi to medial qi by (7/19) / (12) = 7/228 of a mean lunation.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: Since we are counting up the increasing lag in units of (1/228) of a mean lunation, and the Intercalation Remainder is in (1/19) of a lunation, it is clear that the initial multiplication by 12 is needed to convert the Intercalation Remainder to the correct scale, since 12 × 19 = 228.

When the total lag for a given medial qi builds up to greater than 228/228 of a mean lunation, then that medial qi falls after the next mean conjunction, and the lunation preceding that medial qi contains no medial qi at all, since the previous medial qi fell just before the previous mean conjunction.
The month corresponding to that lunation is therefore counted as intercalary;
it bears the same number as the preceding month, with the prefix run 閏 ‘intercalary’.
We then find how many times we need to add 7 to the scaled up Intercalation Remainder until we reach a total exceeding 228.

Having found this number, then if we start counting with winter solstice taken as #1, and if (say) 3 additions of 7 are required to reach 228, the 4th qi will be the one ‘outside the count’ that has shifted onto or past the next mean conjunction.
Suppose for example that the Intercalation Remainder is 14 for this year.
That means the winter solstice lagged 14/19 of a lunation behind the Celestial First Month conjunction.

In order for an intercalation to occur, we therefore need the remainder to increase by 19 − 14 = 5 We multiply by 12 to obtain 60, thus converting the scale from 19 to 228, and then count off sevens from this, each seven representing a medial qi past winter solstice that must pass before an intercalation is triggered.
Now 60/7 = 8, remainder 4 So it will take 9 more medial qi after winter solstice, the first medial qi, before we accumulate the required remainder of 228.
Thus it will be the 10th medial qi that will lag its corresponding (10th) conjunction by enough to take it past the next (11th) conjunction.
The 10th lunation therefore contains no medial qi.
It will thus be counted as the lunation of the intercalary 9th month, and it is the next lunation that will contain the 10th medial qi and thus correspond to the 10th month of the Celestial count.
Of course the intercalary 9th Celestial month is the intercalary 7th civil month;
we reach that number if we start counting from the 11th civil month of the preceding year, rather than the first Celestial month.

What is the point of the statement that we should count a month ‘for each completed four’? This relates to a practice that we have already noted in the period when the Triple Concordance was in use – although as we have seen there is no explicit description in the system itself.
The practice was that if the medial qi falls so near the next conjunction that it actually falls within the same day as that conjunction, then it is counted as falling within the next lunation.
As a result, an intercalary month will be counted one month earlier than would otherwise have been the case.
The ‘completed four’ method gives us a rough and ready way of telling when this shift might be called for.
We may note that:
4/228 of a lunation is (4/228) × (29 499/940) days = 478/940 days to 3 significant figures, just over half a day.
So the ‘completed four’ method places the qi in the next lunation if that qi falls within half a day before the conjunction, so that the current lunation corresponds to an intercalary month.
If the interval is larger than 4/228 but less than 7/228 day, the next month will be intercalary.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §52 Set out years of entry into the Obscuration and subtract one.
Multiply by Extinction Number [21], and obtain one for each filling of the Day Factor [4].
Called this Accumulated Extinctions.
What is not exhausted is Extinction Remainder.
Multiply Accumulated Extinctions by Compat - ibility Factor [487], and count one for each filling of Extinction Factor [7].
Call this the Greater Remainder.
What is not exhausted is the Lesser Remainder.
As the Greater Remainder fills 60, cast it out, and count off the remainder from the Obscuration [sexagenary day] name.
Outside the exhausted count, that is the Extinction Day before the winter solstice of the preceding [civil] year.

To predict the next Extinction, add 69 to the Greater Remainder, and 4 to the Lesser Remainder, and as the Lesser Remainder fills the Extinction Factor [7], let that go with the Greater Remainder, and count off as before.
When there are no fractions, that is Obliteration.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: Since the interval from one winter solstice to the next is 1461/4 days, and this is equal to 360 + 5¼ = 360 + 21/4 days winter solstices do not all occur on the same sexagenary day.
It would however be very convenient if they did.
To deal with this problem, we do something akin to intercalation, by considering a ‘basic’ solar cycle of 360 days, in which all qi are assumed to fall on the same cyclical day as the preceding year.
We then allow for the fact that extra days do in fact accumulate at the rate of 21/4 per solar cycle, so that the cyclical days on which qi fall shift further through the sexage - nary sequence.
The total number of whole extra days accumulated to date is the Accumulated Extinctions.
The question then arises as to when precisely the extra days amounted to the whole number which is Accumulated Extinctions:
that day is the Extinction Day.
Now the number of days in the year is 1461/4, and each year accumulates an extra 21/4 days.
So each day in the year contributes:
(21/4) / (1461/4) days = 7/487 days (So NB that each of the 24 qi contributes (21/4) / 24 = 7/32 days.
Thus each whole day of a qi may be taken as contributing 7 / (15 × 32) days) 487 is the Compatibility Factor and 7 is the Extinction Factor, as indicated.

Alternatively, we may say that each day of Extinction takes 487/7 = 69 + 4/7 days Hence multiplying Accumulated Extinctions by 487 and dividing by 7 gives us the number of days from the start of the current Obscuration to the moment of Extinction.
Since 487/7 = 69, remainder 4, adding these numbers as specified will take us to the next Extinction Day.
If on any given Extinction Day there is no fractional remainder, that is an Obliteration.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §53 Multiply the Lesser Remainder of the winter solstice by 15, and subtract from Compatibility Factor [487].
Obtain 1 as the remainder fills Extinction Factor [7], then that is the Extinction after the Celestial Standard [conjunction].
The Lesser Remainder of the winter solstice is the remainder when years into the Obscuration are multiplied by Day Remainder [168] and divided by Medial [ Qi] factor [32].
It takes on the values 0,8,16 and 24 over a four-year cycle.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: Since one year contributes 21/4 days towards an Extinction, each of the 24 qi contributes (21/4) / 24 = 7/32 days.
So .
each of the 15 days of a qi may be taken as contributing 7 / (15 × 32) days).
So if we have a Lesser Remainder at the usual scale of 32, that has taken [Lesser Remainder] × 15/7 days to accumulate, and that is the time since the last Extinc - tion.
Thus, since Extinctions are 487/7 days apart, the time to the next Extinction is (487 − 15 × [Lesser Remainder]) / 7 days – as specified.
Checking in detail:
The gaps from the previous Extinction to the winter solstice commencing the second year of the Obscuration is:

365 − 5 × 487/7 since there were five Extinctions before the winter solstice = 5 × (73 − 487/7) = 5 × (511 − 487) / 7 = 5 × (24/7) = 15 × (8/7) So the next year the gap will be twice this, at 15 × (16/7) And in the next year the gap will be:
15 × (24/7) And these gaps are in each case (Lesser Remainder for winter solstice) × 15/7.
Clearly therefore we can find the gap from winter solstice to the subsequent extinction by subtracting these amounts from 487/7 as specified.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §54 Set out the Accumulated Months of entry into the Obscuration, multiply by Obscuration days [27,759], and cast out and discard what fills Greater Circuits [343,335].
As for the remainder, obtain 1 for each filling of Obscu- ration Months [940].
Call this Accumulated Du.
What is not exhausted is Remainder Parts.
To the Accumulated Du, add the 21 du of Dipper, with [its] 235 parts, and then for each Lodge cast out in succession.
When it does not fill a Lodge, then that is the du of the Lodge 13 at which the sun and moon are located at their conjunction.
To seek the next conjunction, add to the du 29, and add to the Parts 499, obtaining 1 du as the Parts fill Obscuration Months [940], and casting out 235 Parts as you pass through Dipper.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: Accumulated Months have already been calculated for the conjunction of the first Celestial (and hence subsequent) months in Proc. 3.6.

Obscuration Days [27,759] is the number of days in a month at a scale of Obscuration Months [940], so the multiplication specified produces the number of days elapsed at the instant of conjunction (and hence number of du moved by the sun), including fractional parts, at a scale of Obscuration Months [940].
Greater Circuits [343,335] = 365¼ × 940, so this represents the du in a complete circuit at the same scale.

Casting this out gives the number of du moved by the sun past its starting point at winter solstice – which is also the du moved by the moon at the time of the conjunction, since its position coincides with that of the sun.

If we want to locate the present position of the sun and moon in the lodge system, then we have to take account of the fact that in the system used by the Han Quarter Remainder, winter solstice position of the sun is at 21¼ du of the lodge Dipper.
Thus to count movement of the sun from the start of Dipper we have to add this amount, with the ¼ du in the form 235/940.
We then move through the lodge system casting out the different extensions of each lodge in turn until we find which lodge the sun is located in at the time of the conjunc - tion.
As the text notes, when we pass through Dipper again (which is in all 26 235/940 du across) we must remember to deduct the fraction as well as the whole du of this lodge.
Since the length of a mean lunation is 29 499/940 days, this is also the number of du that the sun moves between conjunctions.
By adding this amount we can move from the position just calculated to the next conjunction position.
13 I emend xing 星 ‘star’ in the original to xiu 宿 ‘lodge’, which is graphically plausible and suits the sense of the passage better.
The received text runs 置入蔀積月以日乘之 ‘Set out the Accumulated Months of entry into the Obscuration, multiply by days’ which is clearly defective.

I emend following the version of Li Rui, which involves only the insertion of 蔀 ‘Obscuration’ before ‘days’, and produces an exact result for the position of moon and sun at the moment of conjunction:

The editors of the Zhonghua edition adopt a more complex emendation, in accordance with the views of Qian Daxin 置入蔀積(月)[日]以(日)[蔀月]乘之 ‘Set out the Accumulated Days of entry into the Obscuration, and multiply by Obscu- ration Months [940]’ :
see Hou Han shu, zhi 3, 3063.
However, this only produces the position of the moon and sun on the midnight of the day on which the conjunction falls, not at the moment of conjunction itself.
Li Rui’s simpler read - ing is clearly preferable.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §58 Set out the number of Accumulated Days entered into the Obscuration, and multiply them by Lunar Circuits [1016].

Cast out and discard what fills Obscuration Days [27,759], and obtain 1 for each time the remainder fills Obscuration Factor [76], which is Accumulated Du, while what is not exhausted is Remainder Parts.
To Accumulated Du add the 21 [ du] and 19 parts of Dipper, and cast out according to the method above, then that is the degree of the Lodges where the moon is located at midnight on the day sought.
To seek the next day, add 13 du and 28 parts.
To seek the next month, for a long [month] add 35 du and 61 parts, but if the month is small add 22 du 33 parts.
If the parts fill the factor obtain 1 du, and in passing through Dipper cast out 19 parts.
When in the last ten days of winter the Moon is in Spread and Heart, take note of it;
this refers to the time between the [end] boundary of the day clepsydra up to the end of the [night] clepsydra.
Lunar Circuits [1016] is the number of circuits of Heaven made by the moon in an Obscuration, during which the sun only makes 76 circuits.
So 1016/76 gives the factor by which the moon’s speed is greater than the sun’s.
Since Accumulated Days is the number of du moved by the sun since the start of the Obscuration, multiplying by this factor gives the du moved by the moon.
Subtraction of Obscura- tion Days [27,759] before dividing by Obscuration Factor [76] removes the whole circuits from the result.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: Clearly the lunar motion for one day is 1016/76 du = 13 du and 28 parts.
From this we may find that the motion for 30 days is:
30 × 1016/76 du = 401 du and 4 parts.
Casting out a whole circuit at 365 du and 19 parts, we reach the figure of 35 du and 61 parts given in the text for 30 days, from which the figure for a short 29 day month follows immediately.
An error is of course introduced by the assump - tion that the month is a whole number of days long.
As Li Rui points out (Li Rui 李銳 (1768–1817) 1993:

761), the final sentence also appears in variant versions in the Uranic Manifestation system that was in use in the kingdom of Wu 吳 from 223–280 ce (see the translation in Chapt er 4, the Uranic Manifestation system, section § 44), and the Luminous Inception system, Jingchu li 景初曆 used in Wei 魏 about the same time.

It apparently refers to a practice mentioned in the Sui shu (25, 702) as having been followed under the Chen dynasty, in which punishments could not be carried out at certain times, including when the moon was in the lodges mentioned.
The point of the passage is to say that this prohibition only applies when the moon is in the forbidden positions during the official hours of darkness.
The occurrence of these words in a description of Han practice suggests that the custom was not limited to the Chen.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §60 Method:
set out the number for the night clepsydra for the Nodal qi of that month, and multiply it by Obscuration Factor [76].
Cast out 200 from it, obtaining 1 part [for each complete 200], then this is the parts moved [by the sun] from midnight until dawn.
If you increase by this the du and parts where the sun is located at midnight, that is the du and parts where it is located at dawn.
Clepsydra runs are given in 刻 ke, each of which is 1/100 day.
So the process described takes half of the night ke, and converts it to parts of a day at a scale of 76.
Since the sun moves 1 du in a day, these are parts of du as stated.

Count one for each full Year Number [513].
This is called Accumulated Eclipses.
The remainder is the Eclipse Remainder.

An Obscuration Coincidence begins with an eclipse at full moon of its first Celestial month, as was the case in the month beginning at System Origin ‘Year of entry’ is the number of the target year in the Obscuration Coincidence;
subtracting one gives us the interval in years from the start of the Obscuration Coincidence to the start of the current Celestial year.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §75 In each case add 27 to the Greater Remainder, and 615 to the Lesser Remain - der.
Where the parts for the month do not fill 20, further add 29 to the Greater Remainder and 499 to the Lesser Remainder.
The Lesser Remainder for the eclipse should be compared with the clepsydra graduations.
Where the night run is not exhausted, count one back to make the day.
The aim here is to predict the sexagenary day and time of day of the next eclipse.
To get to these figures, we multiply the days in a lunation by the lunations from one eclipse to another, on the basis that eclipses can normally be expected at intervals of five lunations:

5 × (Obscuration Days [27,759]/Obscuration Months [940]) = 147315/940 Since 147 = 2 × 60 + 27, we can see that the sexagenary day number must increase by 27, and the extra parts of a day (at a scale of 940) will be 615, as specified.

Recalling that the mean interval between eclipses is 5 20/23 lunations it is clear that the reference to ‘where the parts for the month do not fill 20’ identifies the situation where the interval since the last eclipse is not yet long enough for another eclipse to be expected.
In that case, we simply add a lunation’s worth of days and parts as specified to get to the conjunction of the next month.
The final sentence refers to the practice already seen in Proc. 3.10, where an event occurring during the hours of darkness after midnight is counted as occur - ring on the previous day.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §76 Cast out Year Number [513] from [the years since] High Origin.
[From the] remainder make Accumulated Months, and multiply by 112.
Cast out what fills Month Number [135], and for the remainder obtain one for each filling of Eclipse Factor [23], then this is the eclipse after Celestial First Month.
As Li Rui notes, the start of this text is elliptical.
It is however possible to make sense of the details that are given here if we consider how the first eclipse of a given Celestial year can in fact be predicted.
14 The steps would be as follows:
(1) Cas t out Year Number [513] from years since High Origin.
This removes complete cycles of eclipses, so that we are counting years from the near - est year in which an eclipse occurs at opposition of the first Celestial month.
(2) W e then take the resulting years, and convert them to months, by multiply - ing by 235 and dividing by 19.

We take the whole number result of this, which is Accumulated Months from the start of the nearest year in which an eclipse occurs at opposition of the first Celestial month up to the start of the present year.
(3) No w we multiply by Eclipse Factor [23] and cast out whole multiples of Month Number [135].
The result will be (at the scale of Month Number) the fraction of an eclipse that has been completed between the last eclipse and the start of the first Celestial month.
It will be a number greater than zero and less than 135.
Let us call this Eclipse Remainder.
(4) If w e subtract this number from 135, the result will tell us how far we have to go until the first eclipse after Celestial First Month is complete.
Now each month, 23/135 of an eclipse is completed.
Thus to find the number of months to be counted until the next eclipse is complete will be:
(135 − Eclipse Remainder) / 23 Now what is proposed here is to multiply Accumulated Months by 112 = (135 − 23) This represents the amount by which one month falls short of a whole eclipse.
Then we are to cast out multiples of 135;
each of these multiples is a whole eclipse’s worth:
thus, for example, if we consider an instant at the start of the 10th month of the sequence, when Accumulated Months is 9, we get:
9 × 112 = 1008 1008 mod 135 = 63 7 multiples of 135 have been cast out, meaning we are 7 eclipses short of the number that would have occurred if there had been eclipses at the rate of one a month;
there have been nine months, so there should have been two eclipses so far:
this is indeed the case, since there were eclipses in the first and seventh month.
Each month we move forward increases the total by (135 − 23).
The 135 repre - sents a further eclipse missed in that month, and thus the number of misses normally goes up by 1 a month, as it should.

But from time to time the accu - mulation of 23s passes the total of 135 – and when that happens a month passes without the total of missed eclipses increasing – which is what happens when an eclipse actually takes place.
Further, for a month in which an eclipse actually falls, (23 × Accumulated months) = a multiple of 135.
So clearly (135 − 23) × Accumulated months = a multiple of 135.
For the next month, when Accumulated Months increases by 1, the left-hand side of the equation will increase by 135 and decrease by 23.
The increase of 135 will not affect the result when 135 is cast out.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: Thus to find the next eclipse, we can count up 23 each month until we reach 135.
Now returning to our example, where we had 9 Accumulated Months, from 63 to the next full eclipse missed is 135 − 63 = 72 72 = 3 × 23 + 3 So the number of fillings of 23 is 3.
The next eclipse after the start of the 10th month of the sequence is indeed three months onwards, in the 13th month of the sequence.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §77 Multiply the Lesser Remainder by 12.
First subtract what matches half the factor, to get one double-hour.
As for the remainder, cast out in accordance with the factor, and with the number of counts obtained begin from zi for midnight.
Then outside the exhausted count is the double-hour of occurrence.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: This procedure can be applied to find the time of day of all lunar phenomena, not just eclipses.
The ‘factor’ here is Obscuration Months [940], which is the scale factor for the Lesser Remainder of months.
Multiplication by 12 and division by 940 converts the Lesser Remainder into (1/12) days, i.e. converts the fraction of a day into double hours.
The day is divided into 12 ‘double-hours’, named after the 12 cyclical signs.
The first double-hour is labelled zi 子, and centres on the moment of midnight.

Thus only half of it is actually in the day counted from midnight, and it is for that reason that we begin by subtracting a half-factor, before counting off the whole factors for each subsequent whole double-hour.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §78 Multiply the Lesser Remainder by 100.
Obtain one ke for each time it fills its factor.
As for what does not fill, multiply it by ten, and obtain one fen for each time it fills the factor.
From the accumulated ke, first subtract half the night clepsydra for the Nodal qi entered;
the remainder is the amount of the daytime water filling.
If it exceeds the day clepsydra, cast that out, and the remainder is the amount of the night water filling.
If the ke do not fill half the night clepsydra, then subtract [the ke] from it, and the remainder is the unexpired part of the preceding night.
The crescents and full moons [are counted on] that day.
The Lesser Remainder tells us the fraction of a day (at a scale of Obscuration Months [940] by which a given event falls after midnight.
First we convert this into ke and tenths of ke, at the rate of 100 ke to the day.

The time from midnight to dawn is ‘half the night clepsydra for the Nodal Qi’ in question, and if the interval since midnight is greater than this, we have moved into the hours of daylight, and subtraction will tell us how far we are into that daytime clepsydra run.
If the event is late enough, it will move into the clepsydra run for the next night, and we subtract the day clepsydra run to find out how far that is.

If however the time of the event past midnight is less that half the night length, then we may calculate how long before dawn the event occurs by subtraction, and as already seen in Proc. 3.10, we count the event as having occurred on the preceding day.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §154 As for Conjunctions Remainder, cast out Cycle Rate from it.

In one solar cycle, the fraction of a con - junction that is added is (Cycle Rate) / (Solar Rate) = 4327/4725 for Jupiter.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §157 By the Conjunction Accumulated Lunations multiply Accumulated Conjunc - tions to make the Lesser Accumulation, and further by Lunation Remainder multiply Accumulated Conjunctions, counting one for filling of the Lunation Factor and letting that go with the Lesser Accumulation to make Accumu - lated Months.
What is not exhausted makes Lunation Remainder.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: This is the first of three sections on this topic.

The calculation just specified in Proc. 38 yields the number of whole luna - tions between High Origin and the last conjunction of the planet before the solstice at the end of the present year (Accumulated Months), together with the remaining fraction of a lunation (Lunation Remainder) taking us up to the instant of the conjunction itself, at a scale of Lunation Factor.
Note that Lunation Remainder here refers to two different quantities in succession:

first the fraction of a lunation between planetary conjunctions, and second the fraction remaining when this quantity is multiplied by Accumulated Conjunc - tions, the integral part being removed and added to the total of months.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §159 By the intercalations diminish the months entered into the Era, and cast out 12 from the remainder.
The remainder is the number of months entered into the year.
Start off from the Celestial Standard [month, which is] the 11th [Xia] month, and outside the count is the month of the planet’s conjunction.
If the Intercalation Remainder fills from 224 up to 231, then the planet’s conjunction is in the intercalary month.
The inter - calation may be shifted back and forth, but it is ruled by the conjunction.
When we subtract the intercalary months, we are left with the months in the present year, plus a multiple of 12 months representing whole years.
Subtracting the latter, we have the months in the present year preceding the month in which the conjunction occurs, on the Celestial month count.
Of course the month of conjunction may be an intercalary month itself.
See section § 50 for an explana - tion of the numbers 224 and 231, as well as the reference to shifting ‘back and forth’.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §160 By Obscuration Days multiply the months into the Era, and as this fills Obscuration Months get one to make Accumulated Days.
What is not exhausted is the Lesser Remainder.
As the Accumulated Days fill 60, cast that out, and the remainder is the Greater Remainder.
Count it off starting from jiazi.1, and outside the count is the conjunction day of the month of the planet’s conjunction.
The ‘conjunction day’ here is the day of the solar-lunar conjunction that begins the month in which the conjunction falls.
The procedure is a simple conversion of whole months into days and fractions of a day at a scale of Obscuration Months [940], using the equivalence:
Obscuration Days [27,759] = Obscuration Months [940] We then cast out multiples of 60 from the whole days to find the shift of the cyclical day number from the initial value at High Origin.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §161 By Obscuration Days [27,759] multiply Lunation Remainder, and by the Lunation Factor multiply the Lesser Remainder for the conjunction [i.e. the luni-solar conjunction beginning this lunation], and let it go with [the previous result].
Simplify by 4465, and for what you obtain, get one for each filling of the Day and Du Factor, to make the days entered into the month.
What is not exhausted is the Day Remainder.
Count off the days entered into the month from the conjunction [day], and outside the count is the day of [the planet’s] conjunction.

Lunation Remainder here is used in the second of its two meanings, i.e. the fractional part of a lunation from the solar-lunar conjunction at the start of the month to the instant of planetary conjunction, at a scale of Lunation Factor, which is Cycle Rate × 19.
However, the end result of this procedure has to be in days at a scale of Cycle Rate × 4.
Now days convert to lunations as follows:
Lunations = Days × Obscuration Months [940]/Obscuration Days [27,759] So in this procedure, we start with:
Lunations × (Cycle Rate × 19), then multiply by 27,759 and divide by 4465, to produce:

Lunations × (Cycle Rate × 19) × 27,759/4465 = (Days × 940/27,759) × (Cycle Rate × 19) × 27,759/4465 = (Days × Cycle Rate) × 940 × 19/4465 And since 4465 = 235 × 19, we have (Days × Cycle Rate) × 940 × 19 / (235 × 19) = Days × (Cycle Rate × 4), as specified since (Cycle Rate × 4) is Day and Du Factor.

Turning to the second quantity, Lunation Factor = (Cycle Rate × 19), so multi- plying Lesser Remainder by this raises the scale to Cycle Rate × 19 × 940 And 4465 = 235 × 19, So the simplification by 4465 prescribed changes the scale to Cycle Rate × 19 × 940 / (235 × 19) = Cycle Rate × 4, which is Day and Du Factor as required.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §163 Add one to the years stepped back, and subtract from [the years to] High Origin.
Cast out what fills 80, and multiply the remainder by the Extinction Number [21].
Count one for each filling of the Day Factor [4], to make the Greater Remainder, and let what is not exhausted be the Lesser Remainder.
Count off the Greater Remainder from the jiazi, and then that is the day of the winter solstice for the Celestial first month in the year of the planet’s conjunction.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: What are the ‘years stepped back’? It is clear that the result of:
(Years to High Origin) − (Years Stepped Back + 1) gives the interval in years from High Origin to the winter solstice preceding the conjunction.
We recall that in calculating ‘High Origin’, we were told to include the current year.
If ‘Years Stepped Back’ are the count from the present year back to when the conjunction actually occurred, this makes sense.

Suppose that we find that we are in year 100, but the conjunction occurred the year before the present year, then clearly there was an interval of 98 years from High Origin to the winter solstice before the conjunction.
Why cast out 80? 80 × 365¼ = 29,220 = 487 × 60 So casting out 80 solar cycles removes whole multiples of 60-day shifts of jiazi.
To find out the shift that has occurred, we have to look at the effect of the remaining multiple of 5.25 days.
Extinction Number [21] is the days and day fraction above 360, at a scale of Day Factor [4], since 21/4 = 5¼.
Thus the calculation of the Greater Remainder as given here gives us the shift in cyclical day number.
Lesser Remainder gives us the fraction of a day by which the solstice falls after midnight, at a scale of Day Factor [4].

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §164 By Cycle Rate multiply the Lesser Remainder , and add it to Du Remainder, and let the number of times this [combined] Remainder fills Day and Du Factor go with the Du.
Then this is the number of days after the solstice that the planet’s conjunction [takes place].
Count it off from the winter solstice.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: Lesser Remainder is the fraction of a day by which the solstice falls after midnight, at a scale of Day Factor [4].
Multiplication by Cycle Rate raises the scale to 4 × Cycle Rate = Day and Du Factor, as required.
Du Remainder (like Month Remainder) has two meanings:
The fr actional part of the angular motion of the planet between conjunc - tions, given once for each planet in the initial listing of constants.
The fr actional part of the angle moved by the sun from winter solstice to conjunction.
This is at a scale of Day and Du Factor, as required.
Here we are using it in sense 2.
So adding the two quantities together gives us the amount by which the conjunction falls after midnight, at a scale of Day and Du Factor.
Any whole du are then added to the du calculated above, which are the Accumulated Du for predicting the du of conjunction.
Thus (since the sun moves at one du/day) we have the days elapsed at the conjunc- tion since midnight beginning the day of winter solstice, as required.

For the production of dusk and dawn [centred stars], multiply the du of Heaven by the day clepsydra, and subtract from it the night clepsydra, counting 1 for 200, to make the Determined Du.
By that subtract from the du of Heaven, and the remainder is [the du of the] dawn [centred star].
Add one to the Determined Du to make [the du of the] dusk [centred star].
If there is a remainder, four-fold it;
if it accords with the factor once, that is shao ‘Lesser’, if twice, that is ban ‘Half’ , and if three times, that is tai ‘Greater’.
What is not exhausted, three-fold it;
if it accords with the factor that is qiang ‘Strengthened’ – let it make up qiang [even if] the remainder is [only] over half of the factor.
When there are 3 qiang that is shao, and when there are four shao that is a du.
Two qiang make shao ruo .
[So] you may alternatively make the remainder for the sun’s du into shao and qiang, and add them to it respectively.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: In this section, we are told what observations and calculations were made in order to produce the data in the solar table that follows.
The summary explanations given here may be supplemented by the details in (Cullen, Christopher 2007a).

The first paragraph refers to the two main sources of actual observational data used for the table – an armillary instrument for measuring the sun’s north polar distance, and a gnomon for measuring the noon solar shadow.
These are to be observed on the days corresponding to the 24 qi, the equally spaced divisions of the solar cycle from one winter solstice to the next;
see Proc. 3.49.
In the second paragraph, reference is made to how the figures for day and night lengths at each of the 24 qi are to be calculated.

Actual observations are made at winter and summer solstice (which are the Nodal Qi referred to here), and it is then assumed that the change of each quantity from one qi to the next is in proportion to the change in the sun’s north polar distance.
With reference to the third paragraph, as mentioned in section § 6, a star is ‘centred’ when it crosses the meridian south of the observer.
The use of a clepsy- dra to time the intervals between the ‘centring’ of a sequence of stars was there explained.

It was customary, as here to pay particular attention to the stars seen to be centred at the different seasons of the year – probably because they pro - vided a means of locating a date in the solar cycle without the need for any timing device or measurements of solar shadow.
The procedure outlined here enables us to find the du between the sun’s position and the position of the stars that will cross the meridian at dusk and dawn.
The system of fractions implied in the final paragraph is based on the foundation of the three main divisions shao, ban and tai, corresponding to ¼, ½ and ¾.
These are then modified if necessary by adding 1/12 ( qiang ‘strengthening’) or subtracting it ( ruo ‘weakening’).

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §255 Centred stars take the location of the Sun as the standard, and [their sequence] is accomplished as the sun moves through four years.
Set out the Lesser Remainders for the 24 qi for the year sought, and four-fold them, and as they accord with the factor make shao and tai.

As for the remainder that is not exhausted, three-fold it, and as it accords with the factor make qiang and ruo, with which one subtracts from the dusk and dawn centred stars, and so each will be determined.
Qiang is upright;
ruo is inverted.
When qiang and ruo are subtracted, if the name is the same it is taken off, but if the name is different it goes with it.
If one makes qiang go forward shao is made ruo;
if from the ruo one goes backwards, shao is made qiang.
The tabulated centred stars are those that apply if is assumed that the relevant qi falls at midnight, so that the midnight position of the sun is as tabulated.
In fact this is not generally the case.

Since qi recur at intervals of 365¼ day, a qi that falls at midnight in year 1 will fall a quarter day after midnight in year 2, then half a day after midnight in year 3, then three-quarters of a day after midnight in year 4, until returning to midnight in year 5.
In any given year, the Lesser Remainder for that qi is the fraction of a day after midnight when the qi falls, at a scale of Medial [ Qi] factor [32].

The procedure given here acts, in effect, to produce quarters according to the shao/ban/tai system, followed by the conversion of the remainder into ± 12ths according to the qiang/ruo system, as outlined in Proc. 3.51.
Since the result is the shift in the midnight solar posi - tion, we may apply the same shift directly to the dusk and dawn centred stars positions.
The final sentence is obscure:

the rendering here follows Li Rui, who sees it as referring to the effect of adding qiang to qiang to make shao ruo, which is clear enough, since 2/12 = 1/4 – 1/12, and of subtracting qiang from shao ruo to make qiang, i.e. (1/4 – 1/12) – 1/12 = 1/12.

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §256 From High Origin when the taisui was at gengchen.17, exhausting the 3rd year of the Xiping period [174–175 ce] when the year is at jiayin.51, the accumulation is 9455 years.

commentary_clauses.raw_clause: The reference to a date in the late second century makes it plain that the state - ment just translated cannot date from the time when the Han Quarter Remainder was promulgated in 85 ce.
The year named is however precisely the year when Liu Hong is first said to have been officially consulted on an astronomical topic:
see Chapter 5, § 73.
It therefore seems likely that this text is part of the editorial contributions of Cai Yong and Liu Hong.
9455 = 157 × 60 + 35 and 35 + 17 = 52 Thus, as usual, the ‘accumulation’ which ‘exhausts’ a given year includes both the initial and final years of the interval specified.
This High Origin fell at the winter solstice at midnight beginning December 15, 9782 bce (as usual, in the proleptic Julian calendar), local Luoyang time (JD −1 ,668,469.81250).
This was also the moment of the (mean) luni-solar con - junction beginning the first Celestial month.
The day then beginning was jiazi.1, and the sexagenary name of the year was, as noted here, gengchen.17.
These conditions will repeat at intervals of Origin Factor [4560] years, so that two Origins later we find a closer Origin (though not a ‘High Origin’) at the winter solstice of late 162 bce.
This is the Origin referred to in section § 14.

As noted there, we need to use the High Origin as our starting point if we wish to calculate lunar eclipses and planetary motions, since it is only at the High Origin that we find all the luni-solar Origin conditions fulfilled, together with conjunctions of all five planets with the sun, and a lunar eclipse at the next full moon.
See section § 85 for a calculation of the interval at which High Origin conditions will repeat.

At the interface with [the reign of] Wang Mang, Liu Xin made the Triple Concordance [system], which went back 31 Origins before the Taichu, to obtain a year in which the Five Planets were in conjunction at gengxu.17, and took that to be the High Origin.

We have no clear reference to any one these systems before the later part of the Western Han, and it may be that they are simply later reconstructions rather than ancient survivals.
Those for the Yellow Emperor, Zhuanxu (and hence early Han, as was thought), Yin , Zhou and the state of Lu are as found in other sources such as ( Qutan Xida 瞿 曇悉達 c. 725 ce:

translation_clauses.raw_clause: §260 In the first year of the Guanghe period [178 ce], the Gentleman for Consulta- tion Cai Yong, and the Palace Gentleman Liu Hong added to and continued the Monograph on the Pitchpipes and [Astronomical] System [from the Han shu].
Yong was able in setting out writings, and in the tuning of bells and pitchpipes, while Hong was able in calculations, and in giving an ordered account of the Three Luminaries.
Now I have examined and evaluated their work:
its ideas are broad and general, and [the details of] numerical procedures are succinct and complete.
Therefore I have collected their notes into a first and second chapter, and have let them serve as a continuation of the Former Treatise, in order to show their point of view.
27 25 The civil year that began in spring 161 bce was a gengchen.17 year, 45 years from the start of the Han dynasty.

According to the Triple Concordance System, the winter solstice of late 162 bce fell on December 25, a jiazi.1 day, at about 17:45 local Chang’an time, while the conjunction beginning the first Celestial month fell at 18:00.
The Han Quarter Remainder system simply moved both winter solstice and conjunction back to the midnight beginning that day – not quite one day, but close enough.
At that moment the sun was about 50 minutes past winter solstice, so the correspondence was not bad.
An estimate of the mean conjunction suggests that it fell close to 15:00 on December 25, so the Triple Concordance made things worse rather than better in that regard.
However, what actually mattered was the accuracy of predictions around 85 ce, when the system was adopted, and this was much better.
See Cullen (forthcoming), chapter 6.
26 These are the apocryphal texts much studied in the Western Han:
they are frequently mentioned in Cai Yong and Liu Hong’s documentary collection:
see Chapter 5.
27 Literally ‘to [give] a complete school of thought’.
The word jia 家 ‘house, family’ is the usual word for an intellectual lineage and its doctrine.
For a discussion of the background and contents of Cai and Liu’s documentary collection, see the Introduction to Chapter 5 of this book.
The document whose translation concludes at this point is the ‘second chapter’ referred to in the text.
